title: Web server log forensics
intro:
A breach has been reported against one of our web servers. The Apache access log from the incident window has been exported to `access.log`. Work through the log to reconstruct the attack timeline: identify the actor, trace what they accessed, and extract the evidence they left behind.

The log uses Apache combined log format:
```
IP - - [DD/Mon/YYYY:HH:MM:SS +0000] "METHOD /path HTTP/1.1" status bytes "-" "user-agent"
```

questions.prompt: Before diving in, get a baseline: how many log entries does `access.log` contain?
questions.solutionMarkdown:
```bash
wc -l access.log
# 310 access.log
```

310 entries across the incident window. `wc -l` counts newline characters, which equals the number of log lines for well-formed access logs.

With 310 entries to analyse by hand, you will use `grep`, `awk`, `sort`, and `uniq` to navigate the data efficiently — the same toolchain used in production SIEM-less incident response.

questions.prompt: How many unique IP addresses appear in the log?
questions.solutionMarkdown:
```bash
awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort -u | wc -l
# 4

awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort -u
# 10.0.0.5
# 185.23.45.67
# 192.168.99.201
# 91.108.4.1
```

Four distinct IPs. Three appear to be legitimate traffic sources; one stands out by volume or behaviour. `sort -u` deduplicates before counting — the pipeline `awk '{print $1}'` extracts field 1 (the client IP) from each log line.

questions.prompt: Which IP address made the most requests to the server during this window?
questions.solutionMarkdown:
```bash
awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
# 85 192.168.99.201
# 75 10.0.0.5
# 75 185.23.45.67
# 75 91.108.4.1
```

`192.168.99.201` made 85 requests — significantly more than the other three IPs which all show 75 each (consistent with normal browsing patterns). This IP is the primary suspect: higher-than-normal request volume is a common indicator of automated scanning or enumeration.

questions.prompt: The other IPs' traffic spans the early hours. When did the suspicious IP first appear in the log? Extract the date in `DD/Mon/YYYY` format from its first entry.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
```bash
grep 192.168.99.201 access.log | head -1
# 192.168.99.201 - - [15/Mar/2024:02:31:00 +0000] "GET /robots.txt HTTP/1.1" ...

grep 192.168.99.201 access.log | head -1 | grep -oP '\d{2}/\w+/\d{4}'
# 15/Mar/2024
```

The attacker first appeared at `02:31:00`, well after normal business hours — consistent with an automated tool or an attacker operating from a different timezone.

The legitimate traffic predates this by hours, which means the attacker started from a clean slate (no prior relationship with the server) and immediately began active enumeration.

questions.prompt: How many of `192.168.99.201`'s requests received an HTTP 200 (success) response?
questions.solutionMarkdown:
```bash
grep 192.168.99.201 access.log | awk '$9 == "200"' | wc -l
# 8
```

Field `$9` in Apache combined log format is the HTTP status code. Only 8 of 85 attacker requests returned 200 — the rest hit 400, 403, 404, or 500 responses. This is typical of automated scanning: most probe attempts fail until the scanner finds something that works.

Those 8 successful requests are the highest-value lines to examine next.

questions.prompt: One of the attacker's successful (HTTP 200) GET requests accessed an administrative path that should not be reachable from outside. What was that path?
questions.solutionMarkdown:
```bash
grep 192.168.99.201 access.log | awk '$6 == "\"GET" && $9 == "200" {print $7}'
# /robots.txt
# /admin/config.php
# /api/users
# /api/users?id=1
# /api/users?id=2
# /api/users?id=3
# /api/status
```

`/admin/config.php` stands out — a configuration file under the admin directory should never be publicly accessible. The `/api/` endpoints reveal the attacker transitioned from scanning to targeted data extraction after gaining the admin panel.

A 200 response on `/admin/config.php` means the server sent back its contents — likely including database credentials, API keys, or other secrets stored in that configuration file.

questions.prompt: Identify the tool the attacker used by reading the User-Agent string from any of their requests. What is the tool name (the first word in the User-Agent)?
questions.solutionMarkdown:
```bash
grep 192.168.99.201 access.log | head -1 | awk -F'"' '{print $6}'
# sqlmap/1.7.8#stable (https://sqlmap.org)
```

**sqlmap** is an open-source SQL injection automation tool. Its presence in the User-Agent confirms the attacker was conducting SQL injection attempts against the `/api/users` endpoint — consistent with the injection payloads seen in questions 4 and 5 (`OR 1=1`, `'--`, `SLEEP(5)`).

The attacker made no effort to mask their tool — either through carelessness or the assumption that logs were not monitored. In production you would block this UA string at the WAF and alert on it in the SIEM.

questions.prompt: One of the attacker's POST requests to `/api/upload` included a `flag` parameter visible in the request URI — it was logged by the server. What is the value of that flag parameter?
questions.solutionMarkdown:
```bash
grep 192.168.99.201 access.log | grep POST
# 192.168.99.201 - - [15/Mar/2024:02:34:48 +0000] "POST /api/upload?flag=tide-runner-0x02 HTTP/1.1" 200 128 ...

grep 192.168.99.201 access.log | grep POST | grep -oP '(?<=flag=)[^& "]+'
# tide-runner-0x02
```

The attacker passed a campaign tag as a query parameter — likely as an exfiltration marker or beacon acknowledgement. This value links the upload activity directly to the same campaign tracked in topic 01 (where `hermit-anchor-0x01` appeared in the C2 key file).

Always log the full request URI including query parameters — GET parameters often carry injection payloads, session tokens, or operational tags that are critical for post-incident reconstruction.
